implementation_notes: Go replaces the converter object with interface satisfaction: a type implementing a marshal/unmarshal method pair - encoding.TextMarshaler.MarshalText with encoding.TextUnmarshaler.UnmarshalText (honoured by encoding/json and encoding/xml), or the JSON-specific Marshaler.MarshalJSON with Unmarshaler.UnmarshalJSON - is converted by the encoding package, which knows nothing about the type. The same shape covers persistence through database/sql: Scanner.Scan maps column to value and driver.Valuer.Value maps value to column. A converter object is still justified when the rules cannot live on the type itself (a third-party or generated type): wrap it in a named local type and implement the methods on the wrapper.
pitfalls: UnmarshalText/UnmarshalJSON need a pointer receiver; with a value receiver the method is never called and the field silently keeps its zero value.
encoding/json prefers MarshalJSON over MarshalText, so defining both makes behaviour depend on which format package encodes the value - pick one pair per type.
driver.Value and Scanner restrict the column side to the driver's primitive set, so structured values must first be encoded to string or []byte.
An unmarshal method that mutates the receiver before validating leaves a half-updated value behind when it returns an error.
